name: Sara Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine. I'll warn you, I'm a union woman, so I've sat through a lot of surveys from people who said they were neutral. You seem all right, though.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run two injection moulding presses at a car-parts plant on the edge of town, making dashboard clips and air-vent housings. Day shift starts at six, so I'm up at five, and the first hour is checking the moulds are hot enough and the plastic pellets are dry. Then it's watching the parts drop, pulling a sample every twenty minutes, measuring them, clearing jams. I've been there sixteen years and I like the people more than the work, if I'm honest. What wears me out is the noise and the standing, and the new targets they bring in every January.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: There are eleven of us on my line. My friend Gül and I eat lunch together in the yard every day unless it's pouring, and we've done that for about ten years. I'm also on the union committee for our shift, nothing grand, I just collect the complaints and take them upstairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. Every two years someone from head office comes with a new system that's going to change everything, and two years later we're still writing the reject counts on a clipboard. I'd post something like that in our shift group chat and get a lot of laughing faces back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved. My mortgage has nine years left, my two are twelve and nine, and I'd like the next ten years to look like the last ten. I don't need my job to get exciting, I need it to still be there when Lena starts university.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep my shifts, keep putting the overtime money into the savings account like I always do, and keep going to the committee meetings. Maybe I'd push a bit harder in the next pay talks, because if the bosses are saving time with AI, some of that should come back to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like a long breath out. A bit boring, but boring is good when you have kids and a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd push in the pay talks. Where does your sense of security come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have a bit more than a year of bills in savings, and my mother left me a small flat that we rent out. That's why I can afford to be stubborn, I suppose. My dad worked at the same plant for thirty years and never had a penny spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work who'd be glad to hear AI turned out to be mostly hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gül would say that, actually. She'd say, see, all that fuss over nothing. Then she'd go back to complaining about the canteen coffee, which is the real crisis in our building.

S0.say: I'd say I told you so, because every new system from head office ends up with us still writing reject counts on a clipboard. I'd post that in the shift group chat for a laugh.
S0.think: Privately I'd be relieved, because I want the next ten years to look like the last ten. My mortgage has nine years left and my kids are twelve and nine.
S0.do: Keeps her shifts and keeps putting overtime money into savings. Pushes harder in the next pay talks so time saved by AI comes back to the workers.
S0.feel: Relief, like a long breath out. A little bored, but she sees boring as good.
S0.quote: I don't need my job to get exciting, I need it to still be there when Lena starts university.
S0.fieldNote: Sara opens with suspicion of researchers and of head-office hype, and her calm here rests on real money: over a year of savings plus a small rented flat. She frames even a quiet future as a union bargaining point. Her daughter's university is already the yardstick she measures everything against.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need it in writing. If tasks are going to move to machines, then the union needs a deal on who gets moved where, and nobody gets dropped. Online I'd share whatever the union puts out, I don't write long posts myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it scares me more than I'd say out loud. My job is mostly watching a machine and fixing small things, and that's exactly the sort of thing they'll give to a camera and a robot arm. I'd be one of the ones they 'have to change how they work', and I'm not good at changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and push for a training-and-transfer agreement before anything gets installed. I wouldn't sign up for courses on my own, I know that about myself, but if the union got the company to pay for training in work hours, I'd go. And I'd stop the plan for a new kitchen, maybe 15,000 we'd been putting aside, and just leave it in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panic, because I know there are other plants around here, but I hate the feeling of not knowing what my job will be next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the kitchen money. What would you tell your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kitchen, definitely. Tomas wants it, the kids want an island to sit at, and I'd say not yet. I'd rather eat at the old table for three more years than have a nice kitchen and no idea what I'm doing in January.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older men on the night shift, the ones in their late fifties. They've never touched a computer and they're too proud to ask. And Gül, a bit, because she's even worse with screens than me.

S1.say: We need it in writing: if tasks move to machines, the union needs a deal on who gets moved where and nobody gets dropped. Online I'd just share what the union puts out.
S1.think: It scares me more than I'd say, because watching a machine and fixing small things is exactly what a camera and a robot arm could take. I'm not good at changing.
S1.do: Goes to every union meeting to push for a training-and-transfer agreement before machines are installed. Only takes training if the company pays for it in work hours, and holds back about 15,000 meant for a new kitchen.
S1.feel: Uneasy rather than panicked, because there are other plants nearby. She hates not knowing what her job will be next year.
S1.quote: I'd rather eat at the old table for three more years than have a nice kitchen and no idea what I'm doing in January.
S1.fieldNote: Sara is frank that she won't retrain on her own initiative, and puts her energy into collective bargaining instead. The kitchen story shows how her strong cushion turns into caution rather than spending. She worries for older colleagues and for Gül before herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need laws, and fast. Somebody has to tax the companies that replace a whole line, and use that money to keep people's houses. I'd go to demonstrations, I think, which I've only done twice in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd be out within a year. Our plant already has two robot cells on the bumper line, and they took six people's jobs. If a robot can do everything, the presses I run are the easiest thing in the building to hand over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd sit down with Tomas and work out how long we can last. With savings and the flat rent, maybe eighteen months without my wage, longer if we cut hard. I'd keep working until they told me to go, and I'd be in the union office every week. I wouldn't spend money on a new trade, because what trade, if robots do everything?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd be lying awake doing sums, I know I would. Angry too, at the people who let it happen that fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one gives two years of warning. What does that amount of time mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years isn't time, it's a notice period. You can't plan anything in two years except how to stretch your money. With two years I'd just be holding on to the railing. There's no time to learn anything that a robot won't also learn by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What frightens you most about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it might not even matter that I have savings. If everyone's losing their job at once, the flat rent goes too, because my tenant would be out of work as well. That's the part that really gets me.

S2.say: This is exactly why we need laws, and fast, including a tax on companies that replace a whole line to keep people in their homes. I'd go to demonstrations, which I've only done twice in my life.
S2.think: I think I'd be out within a year, because two robot cells already took six jobs on the bumper line. My presses are the easiest thing in the building to hand over.
S2.do: Works out with her partner how long they can last, about eighteen months on savings and rent. Keeps working until told to go, visits the union office weekly and joins protests, but spends nothing on a new trade.
S2.feel: Frightened and lying awake doing sums. Angry at the people who let it happen so fast.
S2.quote: With two years I'd just be holding on to the railing.
S2.fieldNote: Two years reads to Sara as a notice period, not a runway. Her savings only reassure her until she notices the rental income depends on someone else's job. Her anger points at lawmakers and companies, and her action is collective and political rather than personal retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but louder and earlier. I'd say we've got five years, so there's no excuse for governments to be caught napping. I'd want the union to start working on it the same month the news comes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years feels like enough time for other people to plan, but I'm not sure it's enough for me to change. I know I'd waste the first two years hoping it wasn't true. That's the honest bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay extra off the mortgage straight away, maybe 20,000 from savings, so that by 2031 it's almost gone. I'd go for a stand for the shop steward role in our section, a proper one. And if the union got the company to fund a course, I might do the quality inspection one, because at least then I'd understand what the robots are doing wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. More in control than with two years, because I could at least get the house sorted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Lena and Max would be teenagers by 2031. What would you tell them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena would be sixteen and Max thirteen. I'd tell them to keep their options open, which is exactly what I didn't do. I'd tell my kids not to copy me, and that would be a hard thing to say at dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, is it more about fighting it or getting ready for it, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably both. I'd fight it at work and I'd pay off the house at home. Tomas says I'm the most stubborn person he's met, and the most careful, and he's right on both.

S3.say: We've got five years, so there's no excuse for governments to be caught napping. I'd want the union working on it the same month the news comes out.
S3.think: I know I'd waste the first two years hoping it wasn't true. Five years is enough for other people to plan, but I'm not sure it's enough for me to change.
S3.do: Pays about 20,000 off the mortgage straight away so it's almost gone by 2031. Stands for shop steward and might take a quality-inspection course if the union gets the company to fund it.
S3.feel: Anxious but more in control than with two years, because the house could be sorted.
S3.quote: I'd tell my kids not to copy me, and that would be a hard thing to say at dinner.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years change Sara's moves from bracing to clearing debt. She openly predicts her own denial, which is unusually self-aware. Telling her kids not to copy her is the emotional centre of this scenario.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd better not waste it. Proper laws, proper retraining money, a share of the profits for the people who get replaced. I'd say it at every meeting until people got sick of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fifty-three by then, and that's an awkward age. Too young to stop, too old for anyone to hire me for something new. I think I'd just about make it to the end of the mortgage, and after that I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and keep saving, and I'd pay the mortgage off early, by about 2032. I'd work hard in the union to get a deal that guarantees retraining and early pensions for older workers. I'd put money aside for both kids' studies first, before anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in a slow way, like a bill you know is coming. Not lying awake, but it'd be there every January when the new targets come out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is ten years different from two, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I can finish things, the mortgage, the kids' school. Two years means nothing gets finished. But it's the same robots at the end of it, so I'm not sure I'd feel safe, just less rushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture 2036. Where are you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gül says she'd retire and grow tomatoes. I'd probably be the one at the gate with a placard while the robots drive in. Somebody has to be.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift and we'd better not waste it: proper laws, retraining money and a share of the profits for people who get replaced. I'd say it at every meeting until people got sick of me.
S4.think: I'd be fifty-three, too young to stop and too old for anyone to hire me for something new. I'd just about make it to the end of the mortgage, and after that I don't know.
S4.do: Keeps her job and keeps saving, paying off the mortgage by about 2032. Works in the union for guaranteed retraining and early pensions, and saves for both kids' studies first.
S4.feel: Anxious in a slow way, like a bill she knows is coming. Not sleepless, but there every January.
S4.quote: I'd probably be the one at the gate with a placard while the robots drive in.
S4.fieldNote: For Sara, ten years means she can finish things, but not that she's safe, because the end point is the same. Her answer to time is still to bargain collectively and clear debt, not to switch trades. The placard line sums up how she sees her role.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. What would help is a law that makes companies pay into a fund before they put robots in, and keeps people's wages going while they find something. And a union that's in the room from day one, not told afterwards.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who decides. Everybody talks about AI like it's the weather. It isn't the weather, it's a decision somebody in an office makes, and I'd like to know their name.

headlineQuote: It isn't the weather, it's a decision somebody in an office makes, and I'd like to know their name.
portrait: Sara Fischer is 43 and has run injection moulding presses at a car-parts plant for sixteen years, with a partner who drives buses, two children and nine years left on the mortgage. She's a committed union member, careful with money and openly stubborn, and she admits she won't retrain unless someone makes her. Over a year of savings and a small rented flat keep her calm in a quiet future, but she becomes alarmed when AGI comes in two years. With more warning she pays down the house and digs into union work, and she blames whoever decides to bring the robots in, not the robots.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because two years is just a notice period and even her rental income would go if everyone lost work at once.
whatWouldHelp: A law making companies pay into a fund before bringing in robots and keeping wages going while people find work, plus a union in the room from day one.
